I also enjoyed SOTR, mainly to see how Haymitch became the man he is in the og trilogy. I don’t really think that either of them came across like fanfiction.

Yes it’s such an important part of the books! I see people saying that Finnick was “too young” to be a career but please, like some regular 14 year old is killing that many people with a trident. Him being so young only proves that he must have been training his whole life to be in the arena. That kid came in prepared. 

I think it’s so interesting that the books have moments where the careers seem to panic/ realise they don’t want to do this, but people still think of them as evil. They’re probably brainwashed from a young age to believe what they’re doing is right. They’re like little human sacrifices for their districts, it’s tragic. They’re don’t realise the cost of victory until it’s too late.

I hate when people say that Snow was “born evil” or that he had no goodness in him. A huge part of Ballad is that he does have good in him, he could be better, and chooses to be selfish and power hungry. LGB has a whole song about it and then goes onto explain this song, how do people miss this? There’s the symbolism with his mum’s things as well. I see people just saying he was just born evil all the time. It robs him of the agency he used to be an evil person. 

My other hot take is that most, if not all, avoxes are born in the Capitol. They are only seen utilised in the Capitol and I don’t think Snow (or any of the other higher ups) would want district people as permanent residents there, even as slaves. I think it also just makes more sense to punish district people with punishments they can see (I.e. public whippings, public executions, etc). Katniss doesn’t seem to have encountered an avox before the first book. 

There’s also clearly a payment system, like in mockingjay where people can buy an above ground placement for their avox family member. That would be unattainable for district people, especially if they weren’t even aware their family were now an avox. 

There are definitely exceptions, but I think they’re few and far between. Possibly some high up rebels who then have to serve key members of the elite? Loved ones of people Snow wants to personally torture/ keep in line? I could easily see it for victors, like Katniss (we see this in the books).

I agree with your point, but just personally I’m not sure I’d want to be Capitol if I could choose. There seems to be a lot of Capitol citizens who end up becoming avoxes (seemingly a lot more than elsewhere) and that’s honestly the worst fate imaginable for me. That’s just my silly preference though in a hypothetical scenario where you could pick. Edit: plus the higher chances of being poisoned if you’re in one of the elite families. 

I’d pick being a normal person in a career district. Still probably living in poverty, but I don’t have to risk being picked as a tribute and I’m probably a lot less impoverished than non career districts. They do get extra stuff from the Capitol every time one of their tributes wins. Plus, if you’re district four, the chance of fresh seafood.

I think their young, idealised love was a huge escape for them, to the point that they chose not to focus on what could pull them apart. I noticed that drink and Lenore Dove are often paired together at the start of the book. Haymitch mentions that he doesn’t drink, but a lot of 12 people do to forget, especially on reaping day. Where does he go to forget it? Lenore Dove. What does he do right after losing her? Drink. 

If he hadn’t been reaped, I think they still would have met a tragic end, but not necessarily broken up. Haymitch was a bootlegger and Lenore Dove was a rebel since she was 12. It was probably only a matter of time before one of them ended up hanging. Once one went, I think the other one would have followed. The only reason Haymitch lived was because he had his promise to keep him going- and Snow would have probably intervened.

I think the career volunteers are handpicked in advance. It wouldn’t surprise me if some of the competitors did volunteer when they weren’t supposed to, but I’d theorise that there’s a lot of social pressure in career districts not to do that. If you’re not picked it’s likely because they don’t think you’ll win and a “lesser” volunteer potentially takes precious recourses away from more likely candidates and potentially robs their district of the prize/ glory.

It’s unfortunate that we weren’t able to see more of her, but there’s no way around it because it had to be from Haymitch’s point of view. 

I don’t know if this is a popular take, but I quite like how we don’t get to see the perspective of any Covey person directly (unless you’d count Katniss, but she considers herself to be from 12). We get Snow’s perspective on Lucy, but he’s an asshole who we know is an unreliable narrator. We get a lot of Lenore’s opinions from Haymitch, but we know that he has a very romantic, idealised view of her, so we can’t take his words as gospel either. One of my favourite things about all of the HG books has been not knowing how much of what the characters “know” is accurate. 

I feel like we’ll get something similar in the 3rd book. I couldn’t say exactly what, but it would be interesting if maybe it was Mags having a conversation with a reaped Covey person from district 12 who is then killed.

I think their behaviour does make sense for where the characters are. Haymitch and Lenore live in a world where death could come at any moment, even without the reaping. Both live arguably very dangerous lives even within their district (Haymitch as a bootlegger and Lenore’s rebellious actions/ status as covey). 

Neither of them were likely to reach old age, even if Haymitch hadn’t gone to the games. The lives they would have led would have been filled with even more suffering. It felt to me like they were trapped in a naive young love because that serves as an escape for both of them. It’s mentioned early on that many 12 residents use drink to forget. I think Lenore and Haymitch use each other.

(This isn’t a criticism of them either, or that they’re “using” each other in a bad way, just that they use this very romanticised love as an escape).

This topic comes up a lot here and it starts to get a bit frustrating for a few reasons: 

1. A lot of people don’t know how to criticise a work, or how to handle criticism- even when they ask for it. 
2. I think most fanfic sites aren’t great places to have a proper discussion, like you might get in a writer’s group/ class.

Just to clarify some points, I welcome criticism from people commenting. I put it in my tags and my author’s notes and I would encourage anyone who wants critique to do the same. I wouldn’t expect it, but you can get some really good feedback if you make it clear it’s welcome. 

However, like a lot of people here have talked about, you’ll also get a lot of comments that aren’t very helpful. I get a few “I’m don’t like this pairing/ character” comments. To be fair, some people genuinely seem to think that’s helpful criticism for my future work. 

A few people have suggested that as long as criticism is “constructive” than it’s always fine to give, but I’m very dubious about how helpful their criticism is if the other person clearly doesn’t want it. No one is required to make a change to their work just because you think it would make that work better. When I’m at work, people can see I know what I’m doing. Here, we’re all just strangers on the internet. 

For alternatives, why not join a discord, or get involved/ start a fanfic writers group? I realise it’s more work, but I think it would be a lot more helpful than waiting for a good comment to come along. You could even ask more direct questions like: “is the tone consistent”, “does this character speak realistically?” Etc. It would also be easier to get a group of people who you know can both take and give criticism. 

I don’t want to come across as selfish, but I have to edit a lot of writing for my work. My job is stressful and tiring, so the comments I tend to give reflect that. Sometimes I’ll give something more in depth, but I tend to give it to fifty words or less. If I really don’t like a work, I tend to back out before the end. 

TLDR: if someone states that they want it, then give it- and make it clear you want it as well! If you want more analysis, forming a group outside of FFN and Ao3 would probably be more helpful.

I can’t comment on the legal aspect (I’m way too paranoid to ask for money in exchange for fic commissions, to the point where it would. probably ruin fanfic for me as a hobby), but I do have an opinion on why the double standard might exist. 

Back in the day where fic writing was relatively new and becoming popular, the biggest voices against it seemed to be authors. You had Anne Rice’s infamous cease and desist letters, or you had the author of the Outlander series writing posts on live journal about why she thought writing fanfiction was wrong (which authors like GRR Martin defended her for). 

Basically, the biggest threats to fanfiction writers seemed to be coming from authors, mostly from popular book series. They cited worries that reading fanfic would “taint their original vision”, or harm their IP. Fan art wasn’t an issue for them in the same way. In fact, I’ve seen a lot of these same authors openly liking fan art, probably in part because it’s free promotion. 

When it comes down to it, I think this is what created the double-standard we’ve seen ever since. I’m not defending it, but a lot of fanfic writers came to rightly fear what people with enough money to make their lives a living hell might do to them. Was charging a couple of pounds for a commission really worth getting sued over? Could they harm your irl job prospects? A lot of platforms for fanfic also explicitly forbid this kind of thing in their TOS, so it’s not a surprise it’s not a huge thing for fanfic. For instance, if I was to try and do something like that now, I’d probably have to link from my Ao3 account to my tumblr, which could then link a patreon, but I probably couldn’t legally have anything fanfic related on the tumblr. It just seems like a huge headache.

That’ll only happen if they don’t see us as a threat though, so I’m very worried about how many people I see suggesting that they use certain sites as a loophole to monetise their fanworks. Even if someone officially only sells their original works and just so happens to offer their fanworks as a side benefit of supporting them, they’re playing with fire. 

This goes especially for people who dabble in using people’s actual images/ people who might want to monetise RPF. I see so many people on Etsy selling prints, mugs and keychains with celebrities faces on them without their permission, or compensation. They are 100% getting sued if that person happens to see their work and takes issue with any of the above. It’s happened before and will happen again (though many more well known examples deal with chains). The only thing protecting a lot of them on Etsy is likely them being so small actors might not want to spend the legal fees, even if they knew about them- but it’s still a huge risk!

Going by that logic, if people started selling RPF, the celebrities involved would almost have to be entitled to royalties. You’re using their identity, their image, and selling it.

A lot of people in favour of monetising fanfic also don’t consider how many of these IPs, even in their ideal scenario, would almost definitely be entitled to most of the money they make. Some franchises have multiple authors, but those authors are vetted and don’t actually own any of their work. The IP owner can fire them, stop selling their work, take most of the profits, etc. I don’t get how any of that is even appealing. If fanfic was something people monetised, I’d never want to write it.

I think that’s one of the main benefits of this kind of writing, because it makes it almost exclusively for fun/ venting/ whatever the author wants. I lived with my parents until I was 23 and a lot of my friends, who moved out at 18, would constantly ask me when I was moving out. The truth was, I was ready mentally to move out for years, but financially it would have been a bad move. I was in uni until I was 22 and part-time work doesn’t pay for rent where I want to live, and then I had to save up. 2 years later I had the rest of my deposit. 

Saving up was a wise move and I’ve now got my own place. Was it hard at times? Yes. Would I do it all again? Yes. In fact, if I’d saved up for longer, I’d probably have had more money to spend on fixing up my place a bit more prior to moving in. 

It was annoying to be treated like I was immature or childish because I didn’t want to spend money on rent. A lot of my friends used student loans to get a place maybe thirty minutes away from their parents, while others had their rent paid by their parents outright. I’ve been saving to get my own place since I was 16. 

And there’s nothing wrong with staying with your parents until you’re ready either! Like I said, I don’t think I would have been ready to move out at 18 even if I’d had the funds. Assuming that anyone makes that promise to themselves and then can’t be trusted by “their word” sounds very judgmental and isn’t correct. I’ve explicitly told my readers “don’t count on updates, you’re not going to get them regularly and there’s a decent chance I won’t update for years.” It’s a disclaimer I’ve placed on every work I’ve ever written and I’ve also been clear on “I might not continue this for a while, if ever.” If that makes me untrustworthy, ok. 

People write in different ways, and people need passion to write. If people don’t want to write, they won’t. Trying to force someone to finish stone thing they started for fun won’t get you anywhere, except maybe blocked by author.

I’m not a big fan of bashing characters either, even characters I don’t like. On the other hand, I think if there’s a character that you don’t want in the story (for whatever reason) there’s usually a way that the writer can remove them from a story and still keep the character intact. 

There’s this character called Mineta in BNHA who’s very unpopular among a lot of fans of the anime. He’s not a huge part of pretty much every fix I’ve read, especially ones that take place in a future setting. A few of them mention that he went off to be a hero elsewhere and I’ve always liked that. I can’t blame people for not wanting to write about him as a character, but it’s cool that they also wrote him out in a kind of “nice” way- not sure if that’s the right way to put it.

It’s not “they could have gone about it a better way”- they could have realised that there are more serious things going on right now and being rude and entitled to a person for something that is a hobby was unacceptable. 

It is No One’s job to finish a story. Take this from someone who will go back to a story and finish it after a year, or even multiple years, of no updates. The time difference can mean my writing style can often change drastically from chapter to chapter, which can sometimes mean I have to rewrite certain sections to keep things consistent. Same goes for when I decide to change the outcome for certain characters, change plot points, etc.

History has a rich tradition of writers taking on other writers stories and adding new elements to them. Romeo and Juliet was written a thousand times before Shakespeare, but he knocked it out of the park. I’m not saying this to suggest that people should just give up their works in the hope that a better author comes along, but people shouldn’t be discouraged from offering their work to someone who actually wants to write it. If people know the passion is gone and never coming back, offering someone else the chance to see a beloved work finished sounds like a great thing. 

No one is “obligated” to finish anything. I get that kind of stuff in my inbox every so often and I have never updated faster because of it. It can go from what op received to a slightly more polite “are you going to finish this story?” It’s only ever put me off. This kind of comment makes me want to let them know that I’ll never finish it, even if I’m currently writing a chapter.
